blocks.content: This chapter opens a new module focused specifically on Linux, translating the process, scheduling, and memory concepts covered earlier into the actual system calls a Linux program uses every day. Fork and exec are the two calls behind nearly every new process that ever runs on a Unix like system, and they are almost always used together, in a specific, deliberate two step sequence.

Understanding fork and exec precisely also sets up the next two chapters directly: zombie and orphan processes are both direct, natural consequences of exactly how fork creates a parent child relationship.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785409197682-815249101.png
1. What fork Actually Does

The fork system call creates a new process that is, at the instant it is created, a near identical copy of the calling process. The new process, called the child, gets its own copy of the parent memory space, its own process ID, and its own entry in the OS process table, but starts out running the exact same program, at the exact same point in that program, as its parent.

The genuinely strange and important part of fork is that it returns twice: once inside the parent process, where it returns the newly created child real process ID, and once inside the brand new child process itself, where it returns exactly 0. A single call to fork, one line of code, ends up executing on two separate paths, distinguished only by that return value.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785409197683-914362877.png

blocks.title: Why the return value matters so much
blocks.content: Since fork produces two processes running the exact same code from that point forward, the only way either process can tell which one it actually is, and therefore which branch of logic to follow, is by checking what fork returned to it.
2. Copy on Write: Making fork Practically Cheap
blocks.text: 2. Copy on Write: Making fork Practically Cheap

blocks.content: Naively, duplicating a process entire memory space on every single fork call would be extremely expensive, especially for a process holding a large amount of memory. Modern systems avoid this cost with a technique called copy on write, directly building on paging concepts from the memory management module.

Immediately after fork, the parent and child share the exact same underlying physical memory pages, marked read only for both processes. Only when either process actually attempts to write to one of those shared pages does the kernel step in and duplicate just that one specific page, giving the writing process its own private copy. Pages that are only ever read, which in practice is most of a typical process memory, are never actually duplicated at all.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785409197908-948101018.png
blocks.alt: Copy on Write: Making fork Practically Cheap

blocks.content: 3. What exec Actually Does

The exec family of system calls does something completely different from fork: it replaces the calling process own program image entirely, code, data, and stack, with a brand new program loaded from disk. The process ID stays exactly the same throughout the call, but everything the process was actually running, its code and its data, is completely gone and replaced.

This is why exec is described as never returning on success. If it succeeds, the calling process no longer exists in any meaningful sense, its own code has been entirely overwritten by the new program, so control simply continues inside that new program instead. exec only actually returns to the caller if it fails, for instance because the requested program could not be found or could not be executed.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785409197908-878261682.png
4. The exec Family of Calls

Several closely related exec variants exist, differing only in how the new program arguments and environment are supplied, not in what they fundamentally do. All of them ultimately perform the same underlying replacement.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785409197909-790129643.png

5. Why fork and exec Are Two Separate Calls
blocks.text: 5. Why fork and exec Are Two Separate Calls

blocks.content: It might seem simpler to have one single system call that both creates a new process and immediately runs a different program in it. Unix deliberately keeps these as two separate steps instead, and the reason is real, practical flexibility: everything that happens between the fork call and the exec call runs inside the child, with no effect on the parent at all.

This gap is exactly where a shell configures a command before it actually runs: redirecting standard input or output to a file, changing the child working directory, or closing unneeded file descriptors, all of it happens in the child, after fork but before exec, using exactly the file descriptor and open file table mechanics covered in the file operations chapter. A single combined create and replace call would leave no window for any of this.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785409197909-869152898.png
blocks.alt: Why fork and exec Are Two Separate Calls

blocks.content: 6. The Classic Pattern: How a Shell Runs a Command
blocks.text: 6. The Classic Pattern: How a Shell Runs a Command

blocks.content: Every time a command is typed into a Unix shell, the shell follows the exact same fork then exec pattern underneath. The shell itself calls fork, producing a child that starts out as an identical copy of the shell. That child immediately calls one of the exec variants to become the actual requested program, ls, grep, python, whatever was typed.

Meanwhile the parent, the original shell process, calls wait, forward pointer to the sibling zombie processes chapter for exactly what wait does and why it matters, pausing itself until the child finishes running. Once the child exits, the parent shell resumes and prints a fresh prompt, ready for the next command.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785409197909-384622391.png
blocks.alt: The Classic Pattern: How a Shell Runs a Command

blocks.content: 7. Tracking Which Process Is Which

Since fork returns different values to the parent and the child, and since exec keeps the process ID stable across the replacement, a program always has a reliable way to know exactly who it is at every stage of this sequence, without ever needing to guess.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785409197909-14694661.png

8. Common Mistakes and Interview Angle

["Assuming fork somehow starts the child running a different program immediately, when fork alone only produces an identical copy; a separate exec call is what actually changes what program is running.","Forgetting that fork returns twice, once in each process, and that checking its return value is the only way either process can tell which branch of code it is actually executing.","Assuming exec creates a new process, when it does not, it reuses the exact same process ID and simply replaces what program that process ID is running."]
items: Assuming fork somehow starts the child running a different program immediately, when fork alone only produces an identical copy; a separate exec call is what actually changes what program is running.
Forgetting that fork returns twice, once in each process, and that checking its return value is the only way either process can tell which branch of code it is actually executing.
Assuming exec creates a new process, when it does not, it reuses the exact same process ID and simply replaces what program that process ID is running.

blocks.title: Interview angle
blocks.content: Be ready to explain the classic fork then exec pattern from memory, why it is split into two calls rather than one, and precisely what copy on write means for how expensive fork actually is in practice. This exact sequence is the foundation every Unix shell and process launching mechanism is built on.

With fork and exec covered, the next two chapters look directly at what happens on either side of this relationship going wrong: a child that finishes before its parent collects its exit status, and a child left running after its parent has already exited.
